title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Serous cystic neoplasms of the pancreas are typically benign epithelial tumors characterized by glycogen-rich, cuboidal cells and a distinctive microcystic or “honeycomb” appearance on imaging. These lesions most commonly occur in older adults and are more common in women. Although usually asymptomatic and discovered incidentally, large tumors may cause abdominal pain, early satiety, biliary obstruction, or gastric outlet compression due to mass effect. Malignant transformation is exceedingly rare, making accurate differentiation from mucinous pancreatic cystic lesions critical to avoid unnecessary surgery. Diagnosis relies on high-quality cross-sectional imaging, endoscopic ultrasound, and cyst fluid analysis when features are atypical, with management strategies ranging from observation to surgical resection in select symptomatic or uncertain cases.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Through participation in this course, clinicians can expect to enhance their ability to accurately diagnose serous cystic neoplasms and distinguish them from premalignant and malignant pancreatic cystic lesions using contemporary imaging criteria and endoscopic techniques. Learners gain practical guidance on risk stratification, surveillance strategies, and indications for surgical referral, aligned with current evidence and guideline-based recommendations. The course emphasizes multidisciplinary decision-making, enabling clinicians to optimize patient counseling, reduce overtreatment, and deliver safe, patient-centered care for individuals with pancreatic cystic disease.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Differentiate the diagnosis of serous cystic neoplasms from other pancreatic cystic neoplasms. Interpret signs and symptoms that would lead to surgical resection of pancreatic serous cystic neoplasms. Identify patients with pancreatic cystic lesions who are appropriate candidates for nonoperative management. Communicate interprofessional team strategies for improving care coordination and communication to ensure adequate care delivery and patients. Access free multiple choice questions on this topic.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Introduction
content: Cystic pancreatic masses are frequently identified on abdominal cross-sectional imaging and pose a diagnostic challenge for the clinical care team. Given the incidence and aggressiveness of pancreatic cancer, it is incumbent upon the care team to determine an accurate diagnosis of all solid and cystic masses of the pancreas. Pancreatic serous cystic neoplasms (SCN), also referred to as serous cystadenoma, compose about 30% of pancreatic cystic neoplasms and, unlike other pancreatic cysts, are usually benign (see Image. Serous Cystadenoma in Computed Tomography). [1] [2]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Introduction
content: More commonly, clinicians' attention is focused on mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCN) and intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMN), which have a substantial malignant predisposition. Hence, an accurate diagnosis of SCNs usually avoids the need for surgery and its associated morbidity, expense, and inconvenience. With increased use and advances in abdominal cross-sectional imaging, the detection of pancreatic cystic lesions has increased, particularly in asymptomatic individuals. [3] Differentiation and accurate diagnosis are therefore critical, as prognoses and management vary.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Introduction
content: The most common cystic lesion of the pancreas is the pseudocyst, which typically develops following episodes of acute pancreatitis. Pseudocysts lack an epithelial lining and are therefore considered "false" cysts. In contrast, "true" cysts possess an epithelial lining, making them susceptible to malignant transformation. Additional types of pancreatic cystic masses include MCN, IPMN, cystic neuroendocrine neoplasm, solid-pseudopapillary neoplasm (also referred to as Hamoudi tumor), acinar-cell cystic neoplasm, and ductal adenocarcinoma with cystic degeneration. [4] This review examines the pathophysiology, clinical presentation, diagnosis, and treatment of SCNs.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Etiology
content: The etiology of SCNs remains poorly understood. Genetic mutations are implicated in its development and are the subject of ongoing research. Alterations in the von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) pathway have been described, and SCN is observed in most patients with VHL syndrome. Results from recent studies indicate that inhibin, a gonadal hormone, may be expressed by these tumors and could assist in diagnosis. [4] Detection of Inhibin in cyst fluid analysis strongly supports a diagnosis of SCN.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Epidemiology
content: SCNs account for approximately 30% of pancreatic cystic neoplasms. These lesions are predominantly benign and are more prevalent in women, with a female-to-male ratio of 2 to 3:1. [4] [5] [6] The typical age of presentation is between the fifth and seventh decades of life, with a mean age of 62, and the lesions are more frequently located in the body or tail of the pancreas. [7] Approximately 77% of individuals with VHL syndrome develop pancreatic serous cystic lesions. [8] Coexistence with other tumors occurs in 10% to 15% of cases, most commonly with pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors. [7]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Pathophysiology
content: The pathophysiology of pancreatic SCNs is characterized by benign tumorigenesis, thought to result from the hyperplastic expansion of cuboidal or columnar epithelial cells resembling those of the fallopian tube. [3] Although the precise etiology remains unclear, genetic mutations are also implicated. SCNs lack the specific KRAS and BRAF mutations commonly observed in other tumors, such as carcinomas. [3] [9] These tumors typically develop as cysts and papillae, often presenting as thin-walled, unilocular or multilocular masses filled with clear, watery fluid (see Image. Microscopic View of Cystadenoma).

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Pathophysiology
content: SCNs associated with VHL syndrome may involve the entire pancreas or present in a patchy distribution. The mixed serous neuroendocrine neoplasm, a rare form of serous cystadenoma, is associated with pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors and is also indicative of VHL syndrome. Currently, there is no evidence that morphologic variants of SCNs confer any clinical or prognostic significance. All variants appear to share a similarly low risk of malignancy. [3] [10]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Histopathology
content: Pancreatic SCNs are typically unifocal, round, well-demarcated lesions that frequently exhibit a honeycombed appearance. The cysts are loculated, contain serous fluid devoid of mucin, and are lined by flattened or cuboidal epithelial cells. [11] The absence of mucin is a key distinguishing feature, as mucin is commonly present in mucinous cysts and IPMNs, both of which carry a significant risk of malignancy.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- History and Physical
content: Most patients present without any specific signs or symptoms. [12] In a recent series, only 34% were symptomatic. [2] Pancreatic SCN are often detected incidentally on abdominal ultrasonography or cross-sectional imaging performed for another condition. This finding leads to a diagnostic evaluation. When patients are symptomatic, the most common presentation includes abdominal pain or a palpable mass in the upper abdomen. Less commonly, patients with large cystic lesions present similar to those with pancreatic ductal carcinoma, with abdominal pain, weight loss, and early satiety secondary to compression of the stomach wall by the adjacent pancreatic mass (gastric outlet obstruction).

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- History and Physical
content: Rarely seen findings include obstructive jaundice due to obstruction of the biliary tree (may lead to acute cholangitis) and pancreatic duct obstruction causing pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, ductal dilatation, and recurrent pancreatitis. [12] Single cystic lesions may be confused with pseudocysts, which share similar presentations and imaging characteristics. However, pseudocysts usually occur after an episode of acute pancreatitis or insidiously in cases of chronic pancreatitis and are frequently associated with pain. Large pseudocysts can compress the stomach, duodenum, or bile duct, resulting in vomiting, early satiety, or obstructive jaundice.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Evaluation
content: This century, there has been a 20-fold increase in the detection of pancreatic cystic neoplasms, mainly through cross-sectional imaging such as computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). [13] Evaluation of SCNs relies on laboratory and imaging modalities to differentiate morphological and radiological patterns. The advent of imaging modalities has led to the identification of four morphological patterns of SCN: microcystic, macrocystic, mixed microcystic, and macrocystic with solid components. [7]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Evaluation
content: The microcystic pattern was defined as multiple cysts measuring less than 2 cm, separated by thin fibrous septa, resulting in a honeycomb appearance. Macrocystic type is diagnosed when cysts measuring 2 cm or more are present. [14] Mixed microcystic and macrocystic types combine both microcystic and macrocystic patterns. Solid SCNs are serous tumors without any cystic lesions on cross-sectional imaging. [15] Currently, there is no evidence that morphological differences have clinical or prognostic significance.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Evaluation -- Ultrasound
content: Ultrasound is typically used as a screening examination, upon which SCN usually presents as a well-circumscribed, loculated lesion. The fibrous portion of the lesion is hyperechoic, and the cystic portions appear hypoechoic. In lesions with only a few millimeter-sized cysts (microcysts), the tumor may appear solid due to the numerous interfaces. Areas of calcification also appear hyperechoic with posterior acoustic shadowing.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Evaluation -- CT Scan
content: SCNs are most commonly lobular. [16] [17] They appear hypodense on unenhanced CT because the tumor has a density similar to that of water. Calcifications are seen in up to 30% of serous cystadenomas; a "sunburst" pattern is less common. The central fibrous scar is hyperdense and is generally arranged in a stellate pattern known as a "stellate central scar." After iodinated contrast administration, the fibrous portions will enhance. Serous microcystic adenomas are considered the only hypervascular cystic pancreatic tumors; hence, their enhancement pattern is an important distinguishing feature.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Evaluation -- CT Scan
content: Lesions with fewer fibrous septations show fluid density regardless of contrast administration. Lesions composed primarily of microscopic cysts can appear solid and show homogeneous enhancement after contrast administration. In these cases, as in all other cystic pancreatic neoplasms, MRI can be used to further characterize the lesion. On CT, it is often difficult to differentiate the oligocystic pattern from the mucinous neoplasms. Therefore, serous oligocystic adenomas should be suspected when an unilocular cystic lesion with a lobulated contour without wall enhancement is situated in the pancreatic head. Due to cystic degeneration, macrocystic variants may be mistaken on imaging for pseudocysts or mucinous cysts. [17]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Evaluation -- MRI
content: T1-weighted fat-suppressed imaging typically shows the cystic portions as hypointense, but hyperintense areas may appear if intracystic hemorrhage has occurred. [18] The fibrous components are hypointense on T1-weighted imaging. On T2-weighted images, the cystic fluid-filled components are hyperintense relative to adjacent pancreatic parenchyma, and the fibrous components are hypointense on T2. In addition, calcifications are hypointense on both T1- and T2-weighted imaging, if visible. After gadolinium infusion, enhancement of the fibrous septations is visible in the early and late phases of imaging and persists within the central scar in later phases. MR imaging is more sensitive than CT for detecting fluid, especially microcysts. [19] There is no visible communication between the cysts and the pancreatic duct.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Evaluation -- Endoscopic Ultrasound
content: This modality readily identifies pancreatic cysts through high-resolution imaging. When endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is combined with other imaging modalities, diagnostic accuracy is significantly improved, enabling high-quality imaging and the detection of small clusters of microcysts. EUS also allows for accurate diagnosis in cases misdiagnosed by other imaging modalities. EUS-guided fine-needle aspiration usually provides a definitive diagnosis; however, sensitivity may decrease when an adequate sample for analysis is not obtained. [12] On EUS, serous cystadenoma typically presents as multiple small, anechoic cystic areas with thin septations. Because of the vascular nature of serous cystadenoma, aspirates are thin and sometimes bloody or may contain hemosiderin-laden macrophages. [20] Cytologic smears usually show low cellularity, with cells having clear cytoplasm and well-defined borders.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Evaluation -- Pancreas Cyst Fluid Analysis
content: This includes chemical analysis (amylase), tumor markers (carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), carbohydrate antigen (CA 19-9), mucin), and cytology. Serous cystadenoma typically shows scant serous fluid, low viscosity, low amylase levels, and low CEA levels (<5-20 ng/mL), with variable pancreatic enzyme levels, including amylase isoenzymes and CA-125. Cancer antigen (CA 72-4) levels are also low. Mucin should not be detected.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Evaluation -- Pancreas Cyst Fluid Analysis
content: Cytology reveals cuboidal cells with glycogen-rich cytoplasm. Combining these parameters helps classify these cysts and differentiate SCN from malignant or mucinous cysts. Cyst fluid DNA analysis may reveal a mutation in VHL among patients with VHL syndrome. [21] Positive staining for epithelial markers (keratins) is seen, while staining for CA 19-9, chromogranin A, S100, and p53 is negative. [22]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Treatment / Management
content: Nonsurgical management should be recommended in asymptomatic cases of confirmed pancreatic SCN. Surveillance imaging can be safely recommended given the slow growth rate of these cysts. There is a small risk of malignancy (<2%). [23] Surgical resection should be considered in the management of symptomatic individuals due to rapidly growing lesions (cyst itself vs hemorrhage), large tumors causing mass effect, obstructive jaundice, pancreatic duct obstruction causing pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, or gastric outlet obstruction.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Treatment / Management
content: Surgical resection should be considered when malignancy cannot be ruled out. [24] The surgical approach depends on the location and may include distal pancreatectomy with or without splenectomy, central pancreatectomy, or pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure). Enucleation has been reported to be a safe option for well-selected patients with serous cystadenoma, preserving endocrine and exocrine pancreatic function, but it is rarely used. [25]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Differential diagnosis of pancreatic cystic lesions is often challenging, particularly when relying solely on radiological studies. Pseudocysts represent the most common type of pancreatic cyst, whereas pancreatic cystic neoplasms are less frequent and are classified as neoplastic. Distinguishing benign serous lesions, MCNs, and malignant mucinous lesions, such as mucinous cystadenocarcinoma, can be complex. The use of radiologic, morphologic, and laboratory tests is critical for differentiating these lesions prior to resection and for evaluating their malignant potential. Accurate differentiation between pseudocysts and serous lesions is also crucial for planning appropriate surgical management. [13] [26]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Rare cystic pancreatic lesions include cystic islet cell tumors, papillary cystic lesions, and lymphoepithelial cysts. The differential diagnosis for serous cystadenomas includes the following entities: Non-neoplastic pancreatic cysts include true cysts, retention cysts, mucinous non-neoplastic cysts, lymphoepithelial cysts, and pseudocysts. Pancreatic cystic neoplasms comprise MCNs, IPMNs, and solid pseudopapillary neoplasms. Cystic degeneration may also occur in solid pancreatic tumors such as ductal carcinoma, acinar cell carcinoma, and endocrine tumors. [13] [26]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Surgical Oncology -- Pancreatic head and uncinate process lesions
content: Tumors in the pancreatic head traditionally require pancreaticoduodenectomy (eg, Whipple procedure) or pylorus-preserving pancreaticoduodenectomy when resection is indicated. The classic Whipple procedure involves en bloc removal of the pancreatic head, duodenum, distal common bile duct, gallbladder, and distal stomach with reconstruction via pancreaticojejunostomy, hepaticojejunostomy, and gastrojejunostomy. Pylorus-preserving modifications maintain gastric function and may reduce dumping syndrome and marginal ulceration.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Surgical Oncology -- Pancreatic head and uncinate process lesions
content: Given the benign nature of SCNs, parenchyma-sparing alternatives should be considered in appropriately selected patients. Enucleation may be feasible for small, peripherally located lesions that are sufficiently distant from the main pancreatic duct, thereby preserving functional parenchyma and avoiding the morbidity of formal pancreaticoduodenectomy. Central pancreatectomy is another option for select neck lesions, though it carries a higher fistula rate. [27]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Surgical Oncology -- Pancreatic body lesions
content: Central pancreatectomy (middle segment pancreatectomy) offers a parenchyma-sparing option for tumors of the pancreatic body, resecting the involved segment while preserving the pancreatic head and distal tail. This technique maintains endocrine and exocrine function but creates two transection surfaces, resulting in pancreatic fistula rates of 30% to 50%. [28] Patient selection is critical, favoring younger individuals with adequate pancreatic tissue on both sides of the lesion and a low tolerance for perioperative risk in potential fistula management. Distal pancreatectomy extending from the tumor to the tail provides a single anastomosis or staple line and lower fistula rates but sacrifices more functional parenchyma. The choice between these approaches requires individualized assessment of tumor location, patient age, comorbidities, and surgeon experience. [27]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Surgical Oncology -- Pancreatic tail lesions
content: Distal pancreatectomy is the standard approach for SCNs in the pancreatic tail, with splenectomy or spleen preservation depending on tumor characteristics and vascular anatomy. Spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy avoids the immunologic and infectious complications of splenectomy and is preferred when technically feasible. The Warshaw technique ligates splenic vessels while preserving splenic perfusion through short gastric and left gastroepiploic collaterals. Alternatively, splenic vessel preservation maintains normal vascular anatomy but requires meticulous dissection of the splenic artery and vein from the pancreatic parenchyma. Splenic preservation is contraindicated when tumor adherence to splenic vessels precludes safe dissection or when malignancy cannot be excluded. [27]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Surgical Oncology -- Enucleation and Parenchyma-Sparing Techniques
content: Enucleation represents the ultimate parenchyma-sparing approach, removing only the tumor while preserving surrounding pancreatic tissue. This technique is most appropriate for small, well-encapsulated SCNs located peripherally with at least 2 to 3 mm separation from the main pancreatic duct on preoperative imaging. Intraoperative ultrasound confirms duct relationships and guides the dissection plane.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Surgical Oncology -- Enucleation and Parenchyma-Sparing Techniques
content: The pseudocapsule surrounding SCNs typically facilitates enucleation, though the microcystic architecture may make complete removal challenging. Pancreatic fistula rates following enucleation range from 20% to 40%, reflecting the exposed parenchymal surface, though most fistulas are low-grade and managed conservatively. Enucleation preserves endocrine and exocrine function, avoiding diabetes and exocrine insufficiency that may follow formal resection, making it particularly attractive in younger patients. [27]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Surgical Oncology -- Outcomes
content: Surgical resection of SCNs is curative in nearly all cases, given their benign nature. Perioperative mortality at experienced centers is less than 2% for distal pancreatectomy and 2% to 4% for pancreaticoduodenectomy. Major morbidity rates range from 20% to 40%, depending on procedure type and patient factors, with pancreatic fistula representing the predominant complication.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Surgical Oncology -- Outcomes
content: Long-term survival following resection of benign SCNs is comparable to that of age-matched population controls. The exceedingly rare serous cystadenocarcinoma carries a more guarded prognosis, though outcomes remain better than pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma given its indolent biology. Recurrence following complete resection of benign SCNs is essentially unreported, and routine surveillance imaging is unnecessary unless histopathology reveals unexpected findings. [27]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Staging
content: If a rare malignant SCN is diagnosed, staging is performed in accordance with the National Cancer Center Network pancreatic adenocarcinoma guidelines.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Prognosis
content: SCNs are benign with a low malignant potential (<1%). In a long-term follow-up study of patients with SCN, morphologic changes were observed in 17% of patients. Overall, 50% had tumor enlargement, and in the remaining cases, there was no change in size. The median growth rate was 0.29 cm per year. [29] The prognosis for patients with SCNs is excellent. SCN should be followed up on regularly because long-term data are rare, and recommendations are updated based on evidence. [30]

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Complications
content: Clinicians must evaluate the risks and benefits of surveillance imaging versus surgical resection. Pancreatic resections are associated with high morbidity (40%–60%) and mortality (2%–5%). [30] Pancreatic surgical morbidity in the short and long term remains high, with pancreatic fistula formation and exocrine or endocrine (diabetes mellitus) pancreatic insufficiency reported in around one-third of cases. [3] When SCNs are not resected, they rarely lead to complications that may warrant surgical intervention, such as pancreatitis, obstructive jaundice due to biliary obstruction, cholangitis, pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, or gastric outlet obstruction.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Since SCNs are benign, it is important to educate and reassure patients. Most cases are found by chance during imaging. Knowing a patient’s personal and family history, such as past pancreatitis or genetic conditions like VHL syndrome, can help guide care. Patients should be encouraged to report new symptoms like jaundice, abdominal pain, or early fullness, as these may need further evaluation for possible complications. Regular follow-up imaging should also be emphasized, as it can affect outcomes if the tumor grows or shows signs of dysplasia.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Pearls and Other Issues
content: Pearls and other issues include the following: SCNs are rarely malignant, unlike their mucinous counterparts (MCNs and IPMNs). The most common cystic lesion of the pancreas is a pseudocyst, a benign entity usually resulting from pancreatitis. Surgery is usually only considered for SCN if symptoms are present (jaundice, gastric outlet obstruction) or if the diagnosis is unclear. The presence of mucin in a pancreatic cyst on fine-needle aspiration is a concerning sign and excludes SCN.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Optimal management of pancreatic SCNs requires coordinated collaboration among multiple specialists to navigate the complex decision-making between surveillance and surgical intervention. Gastroenterologists typically initiate evaluation after an incidental finding on cross-sectional imaging, performing endoscopic ultrasound with cyst fluid analysis to characterize lesion morphology and exclude mucinous neoplasms. Radiologists with expertise in pancreatic imaging provide critical diagnostic input, distinguishing microcystic and macrocystic variants and monitoring growth patterns during surveillance. Pancreatic surgeons evaluate candidates for intervention, selecting appropriate procedures based on tumor location and patient factors while weighing operative risks against the low malignant potential of these lesions.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Pathologists contribute essential diagnostic information through cytologic interpretation of cyst fluid aspirates and histopathologic examination of resected specimens, with immunohistochemistry and molecular analysis available when differentiation from other cystic neoplasms proves challenging. Advanced practice clinicians and nursing staff facilitate care coordination, ensure appropriate surveillance intervals are maintained, and promptly communicate interval changes to the multidisciplinary team. Primary care clinicians play a vital, longitudinal role in reinforcing adherence to surveillance and recognizing new symptoms that may warrant expedited specialty evaluation.

title: Serous Cystic Neoplasms of the Pancreas -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Multidisciplinary tumor board discussion optimizes management decisions, particularly for cases involving diagnostic uncertainty, symptomatic progression, or significant growth. Clear communication among team members regarding surveillance protocols, intervention thresholds, and patient preferences ensures consistency in care delivery. Shared decision-making with patients, emphasizing the benign nature of most SCNs and the risks of pancreatic surgery, aligns treatment plans with individual values and goals. This interprofessional approach minimizes unnecessary surgical intervention while ensuring timely treatment when indicated, ultimately improving patient outcomes and reducing healthcare resource utilization.
